Events, Not Pixels: Where World Models Get the Return Wrong

Haoyue Liu Affiliation: School of Science and Engineering, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen Affiliation: Shenzhen Future Network of Intelligence Institute (FNii-Shenzhen)    Xiaoying Tang Affiliation: School of Science and Engineering, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen Affiliation: Shenzhen Future Network of Intelligence Institute (FNii-Shenzhen) Affiliation: Guangdong Provincial Key Laboratory of Future Networks of Intelligence, CUHK(SZ)*Corresponding author.
Abstract

World models are increasingly used for planning, where a planner ranks candidate actions by returns imagined by the model. However, these models are judged mainly by how well they render frames, even though a visually faithful rollout can still assign the wrong return. To identify where this mismatch arises, we introduce a transition-level diagnostic that replaces imagined transitions with real ones and measures the reduction in return error against a budget-matched random control. Our analysis yields two findings. (1) Event transitions, the few steps where a reward is earned or an episode ends, are rendered as well as other steps (median pixel-error ratio 0.85), yet restoring them removes a median of 70% of the return error. In contrast, restoring transitions with the largest MSE, SSIM or LPIPS error removes less than a random choice. Across the 44 Atari-100k model–collection pairs that pass our reliability checks, including three released families, event patches outperform random patches in 39 (sign test p=1.4×10−7p=1.4\times 10^{-7}{}), with a median gain of +44 percentage points. (2) The remaining error is structured: a complementary patch separates errors at true events from those elsewhere, while an eight-step timing tolerance recovers few events missed by our deterministic models. This structure also guides repair: a rule recorded before four repair outcomes were known predicts when a diffusion model repairs these failures. Event patches improve plan ranking, and the same concentration appears on control tasks with rare reward events.

1 Introduction

World models let an agent imagine the consequences of an action before taking it [18]. A planner rolls candidate action sequences forward inside the model and acts on the ordering of their imagined returns [11, 20, 48, 23, 22, 2, 36]. Released pixel world models support this pipeline in Atari, continuous control, and manipulation [12, 60, 52], and their progress is mainly measured by how faithfully they render the future [59, 65, 53].

Rendering quality, however, is only loosely tied to what a planner needs. A return often hinges on a few transitions that carry a reward or end an episode, so a model can render a rollout well yet misprice it by missing a single paddle contact. Model-level studies expose this mismatch: rankings by visual quality can disagree with rankings by task success [33, 64], and whole-model oracle substitutions find that average prediction accuracy does not consistently explain planning performance [41, 49, 7]. Yet neither these analyses nor compounding-error bounds [26] reveal where that error occurs: is it spread across all sixty steps of a rollout, or concentrated in only a few? We therefore ask:

Where inside an imagined rollout does the error that changes a planner’s decision occur?

To answer this question, we introduce a transition-level substitution diagnostic (Fig. 1). Each imagined rollout is paired with a real rollout that starts from the same context and follows the same recorded actions, so the two differ only in who drew the frames. A frozen, memoryless detector, trained once per game, reads reward and termination from each pair of consecutive frames; replacing one imagined pair with the real one therefore changes the return only at that step. We patch the pairs at true events, the same number of random pairs, all non-event pairs, or every pair. These four patches isolate the targeting effect, its budget-matched control, the error away from events, and an all-real reference.

Our analysis yields two findings. First, return error concentrates at events that do not look wrong. In Fig. 1D, restoring three transitions around a Seaquest reward removes almost all return error; three random ones remove little. Across 44 reliable Atari model–collection pairs, event patches beat random patches in 39 by a median of +44 points, and the advantage appears within a few patches (Fig. 2). Event frames are rendered as well as others (median pixel-error ratio 0.85), yet restoring them removes a median of 70% of the return error; the same pattern holds on eighteen games added after our predictions were recorded. Second, the remaining error is structured rather than merely mistimed. Complementary patches separate errors at true events from errors elsewhere, and timing-tolerant recall shows that temporal offset explains little of the events our deterministic models miss. This structure also predicts where a diffusion model helps; event patches improve plan ranking and carry over to control tasks with rare reward events.

We summarise our contributions as follows:

  • •

    We introduce a per-transition substitution diagnostic with a budget-matched random control. It treats the world model as a black box, and we apply it to three released model families on all 26 Atari-100k games.

  • •

    We show, for the first time on released pixel world models, that return error concentrates at reward and termination transitions, also under each model’s own reward head and without the score display, and that a complementary patch separates errors at true events from other errors.

  • •

    We show that a temporal offset explains little of the events missed by deterministic models, predict all four repair outcomes with a rule recorded in advance, and show that event patches improve plan ranking in every counted pair and carry over to control tasks with rare reward events.

2 Related Work

Pixel world models support prediction and control in games [40, 10, 29, 21, 46, 66, 36, 37, 2, 12] and interactive video simulators [62, 6, 54, 60]. Yet visual fidelity can diverge from physical correctness [38] and task success [33, 64, 58]; the same disconnect appears for training likelihood [31, 13, 16], synthetic training data [1], and token pruning [57]. Concurrent work weights error by decision-relevant state dimensions [56], while DIAMOND shows that visual details matter [2]. We instead locate where decision-relevant error occurs inside a rollout.

Oracle substitution localises such failures. Cloning Deterministic Worlds [61] substitutes true states for learned representations, while whole-model oracle interventions relate accuracy to planning [41, 49, 7]; a concurrent diagnostic uses a kinematic null [47]. Closest to ours, counterfactual debugging [32] assigns Shapley credit over time steps to a policy’s sim-to-real gap under injected faults, and agent explanations identify steps that decide a return [17, 8, 3]. We instead operate directly on released world-model rollouts, replacing individual transition pairs under a budget-matched random control. This brings perturbation-based attribution [63, 14, 44, 25], used and tested on Atari agents [15, 4], from pixels to time steps.

Other work improves prediction with multi-step training [50, 55], goal-aware objectives [39], keyframe targets [27, 43], region- and event-aware objectives [34, 42], causal rollout structure [67], and architecture-level probing [28]. Conditional-mean effects are also studied in video prediction [35] and perception and driving models [45]. We test which explanation accounts for missed events using event survival, a diffusion model, and the same network trained deterministically.

3 Diagnostic Setup

The diagnostic needs only rendered frames, so it applies to released checkpoints without access to their internals.

Return from a Predicted Trajectory.

A probe is a real context with fixed actions a1:Ha_{1:H} (Fig. 1A); from it, a model produces imagined observations o^1:H\hat{o}_{1:H}. A frozen detector, shared by all world models of a game, reads each transition pair and its action as a reward sign and a termination flag, (r^t,d^t)=D⁡(o^t,o^t+1,at)(\hat{r}_{t},\hat{d}_{t})=D(\hat{o}_{t},\hat{o}_{t+1},a_{t}) for t<Ht<H; the last frame has no successor, so r^H=d^H=0\hat{r}_{H}=\hat{d}_{H}=0. The emulator, replaying the same actions, supplies r1:Hr_{1:H} and d1:Hd_{1:H}, and both returns stop at the first termination. Rewards enter through their sign, as in Atari-100k training, so all games share one scale:

G^=∑t=1Hγt−1​sgn⁡(r^t)​∏j<t(1−d^j),E=𝔼​|G^−G|,\hat{G}=\sum_{t=1}^{H}\gamma^{t-1}\operatorname{sgn}(\hat{r}_{t})\prod_{j<t}(1-\hat{d}_{j}),\quad E=\mathbb{E}\lvert\hat{G}-G\rvert, (1)

where GG is computed in the same way from rr and dd, and 𝔼\mathbb{E} averages over probes. Atari uses H=60H=60 and γ=0.99\gamma=0.99.

Substitutions and Their Controls.

For channel cc (observation oo, reward rr or termination dd) and a binary mask mm, let G^c,m\hat{G}^{c,m} be the return after substituting the selected real information (Fig. 1). Observation patches replace both frames of the selected transition before detection, so no pair mixes real and generated frames; unselected pairs keep their predictions. Reward and termination interventions replace r^\hat{r} or d^\hat{d}. We report the fractional reduction in mean absolute return error:

R⁡(c,m)=1−𝔼⁡[|G^c,m−G|]𝔼⁡[|G^−G|].R(c,m)=1-\frac{\mathbb{E}[|\hat{G}^{c,m}-G|]}{\mathbb{E}[|\hat{G}-G|]}. (2)

The all-frame value R⁡(o,𝟏)R(o,\mathbf{1}) measures performance when the detector sees only real transition pairs.

The event mask starts from nonzero real reward or termination and is dilated by one step, i.e., the transitions just before and after are also selected, to cover delays in the visual markers. We report its realised coverage q=𝔼⁡[H−1​∑tmtev]q=\penalty\mathbb{E}[H^{-1}\sum_{t}m_{t}^{\rm ev}], which includes dilation. The random mask selects the same number of steps in each rollout. The targeting advantage is

L=R⁡(o,mev)−R⁡(o,mrnd).L=R(o,m^{\rm ev})-R(o,m^{\rm rnd}). (3)

The complementary mask m¯ev\bar{m}^{\rm ev} measures errors away from the selected events, and its contrast with the event patch classifies the failure pattern of each model.

4 Localising the Return Error

We localise the return error with one frozen, memoryless detector per game, shared by every world model of that game. A random patch also hits true events, and more of them as coverage grows, so the lift of Eq. (3) credits the event patch only with what it adds beyond chance.

Figure 2 widens the event neighbourhood step by step and plots the lift against the resulting coverage. In 8 of 9 sweeps over three games and three released families, the event curve stays well above the random curve. For DIAMOND on Freeway, patching 2.8 of sixty steps removes 69% of the error, against −4-4{}% for random patches and 86% when every frame is real; on Pong, 2.1 steps remove 43% against 5%. The sweep also exposes a timing effect: without dilation the Freeway event patch is negative, consistent with the reward digit appearing after the transition that earns it, so we treat the neighbourhood as part of the measurement.

The sweep also shows why the random control is needed. For DIAMOND and Simulus on Seaquest, both patches remove more error as coverage grows while the lift stays flat, so the event-patch reduction alone would overstate the targeting effect. Table 1 reports every game at a one-step neighbourhood, and Fig. 3 shows events beyond Atari.

5 Missing Events and a Model-Class Repair

Localisation shows where the return error lies, not why. We ask why imagined events are missed and whether another model class draws them.

5.1 Absent or Mistimed Events

A detector can miss an event in imagined frames for two reasons: the model draws it at a neighbouring step, or it does not draw it in a form the detector reads. The two predict different curves. If events are only mistimed, recall should rise with the alignment tolerance faster than for a displaced-prediction null; if they are not drawn readably, recall should stay low at every tolerance.

5.2 A Rule Recorded Before the Outcomes

If events are not drawn readably, a model that draws them should reduce the return error, most where the baseline misses most events. As a repair, we replace our deterministic MSE predictor with a diffusion model trained on the same data [24, 30, 2], which samples each next observation instead of regressing it (“sampling” in figures and tables). A sampled future can differ from the realised one, so we evaluate event recall, return error, and plan ranking.

Before observing the remaining outcomes, we pre-specified this rule: a baseline event recall at τ=0\tau=0 below 0.500.50 predicts a return-error reduction larger than the declared floor of that game, and a recall at or above 0.500.50 predicts no such reduction. The threshold is a heuristic for the headroom left by missing events; floors and failure conditions were fixed at the same stage. Freeway had already been scored, so the prospective score covers Pong and the three unrun sampling arms. The MSE baseline gets more training, 30k updates against 8k, because at 8k updates it detects no return on Freeway and Pong; data, sequence length, batch size, learning rate, and seeds match (supplement).

6 Experiments

In this section, we carry out experiments to address the following questions: Q1: Is the return error concentrated at event transitions (Sec. 6.2)? Q2: Are missed events absent or only mistimed (Sec. 6.3)? Q3: Does a diffusion model repair them as recorded (Sec. 6.4)? Q4: Do the same transitions drive plan selection (Sec. 6.5)?

6.1 Experimental Setup

We study 26 Atari games [5] with 64×6464\times 64 observations and frameskip four, using Atari-100k [29] model checkpoints [2, 36, 12]. Across three released families and three locally trained random-policy Breakout models, 44 pairs clear reliability checks. Transfer evaluation adds 9 rows across 6 DeepMind Control tasks [51] and released iVideoGPT on robosuite [68, 60, 52].

Atari attribution uses 400 probes, each paired with a real trajectory under the same actions. Each frozen detector must reach a reward-event F1 of 0.900.90 on an independent collection with environment seeds disjoint from its training data. Terminations are read but not gated; replacing them removes a median 0.7% of the return error. The real reward at the last step stays in the all-real residual (median 1.5% of the error; supplement). Figure 7 adds matched-action RSSM [20] and Transformer predictions on MiniGrid [9] and Crafter [19].

6.2 A1: Return Error Concentrates at Events

Main Results. As shown in Table 1, the event patch has positive lift in 39 of 44 counted pairs (sign test p=1.4×10−7p=1.4\times 10^{-7}{}), with a median of +44 points (probe-bootstrap 95%95\% intervals: 38 above zero, 2 spanning it, 4 below). Each released family and every counted game except MsPacman has a positive median lift (per-game sign test, p=5.2×10−4p=5.2\times 10^{-4}{}); three sampling seeds change lift by a median of 2.0 points, and other discounts and horizons keep 39–41 pairs positive (supplement). As a patch changes only the selected transitions, event transitions cause most of the return error.

Robustness to the Reward Reader. To rule out our detector, we use each model’s reward head: all 25 pairs whose head reads real futures reliably stay positive (median +46; rank correlation 0.85 with our detector), as do 6 pairs from games it cannot read. Hiding the score display keeps all 6 Pong and Freeway pairs positive (median +64; supplement).

Comparison with Pixel Error. One may expect the error to sit in poorly rendered frames. Yet event frames are rendered as well as other frames (median ratio 0.85), and as shown in Table 2, the transitions with the largest MSE, SSIM or LPIPS error are events only about as often as random picks, so patching them removes less than random patches. Pixel metrics thus cannot locate the return error.

Effect of Coverage. Random patches hit more events as qq grows, so a lift that only reflected sparse events would vanish. Yet the median lift is +40 above q=12%q=12\% (+59 below 6%6\%), and all Krull pairs stay positive at q=58.5%q=58.5\%.

Failure Patterns. With Rev=R⁡(o,mev)R_{\rm ev}=R(o,m^{\rm ev}) and the complementary patch’s Rnon=R⁡(o,m¯ev)R_{\rm non}=R(o,\bar{m}^{\rm ev}), a pair is event-dominated if Rev−Rnon>0.20R_{\rm ev}-R_{\rm non}>0.20, non-event-dominated if it is below −0.20-0.20, and unclassified otherwise; the counts are 33, 5 and 6. Simulus on Freeway is event-dominated: event patches remove 72%72\% and the complement −16%-16\%. DIAMOND on Boxing is the opposite: it imagines a return of 6.676.67 against a true 2.312.31, and event patches remove 12%12\% and the complement 72%72\%, so under our detector its excess return lies away from true scoring events. Under its own reward model, it is event-dominated (supplement). Most pairs thus fail by missing true events.

6.3 A2: Missed Events Persist Under Tolerance

We next ask whether missed events are merely mistimed (Sec. 5.1). To investigate this, we compare reward-event recall at alignment tolerance τ\tau with a circularly displaced copy of the predictions, which keeps their event rate. If events were only mistimed, widening τ\tau would recover most of them. As shown in Figs. 4 and 5, it recovers few: on Freeway, the MSE baseline recovers 0.091 of the events at τ=0\tau=0 and 0.153 at τ=8\tau=8, against 0.028 for the null, and across the five games at least 76% of its recall deficit remains at τ=8\tau=8. Most missed events are thus absent rather than mistimed. DIAMOND on Freeway recovers more (0.767 to 0.932), and the diffusion model already reaches 0.943 at τ=0\tau=0.

6.4 A3: A Diffusion Model Repairs as Predicted

If missing events cause the return error, a model that draws them should reduce it. As shown in Table 3, all four comparisons clear their floors, and the pre-specified rule scores 4/4, including 3/3 on the games whose detector passes the attribution gate. Three sampling seeds on Freeway and Pong give error ranges of 0.0356 and 0.0278, both below Δ​E\Delta E.

Ablation on Sampling. A natural question is whether the gain comes from sampling. To isolate it, we train the same diffusion network with a deterministic squared-error objective (same data, 8k updates and seeds). It still has lower error than our MSE baseline on all five games and keeps Freeway’s events (recall 0.95 against 0.94); its seed-mean error is lower than with sampling on Freeway (0.096 against 0.171) and within the larger seed span on the other four, while sampling recalls more events on Pong (0.80 against 0.69; supplement). The repair thus comes from the diffusion network, not from sampling or the training loss.

6.5 A4: Event Transitions Drive Plan Selection

Finally, if events decide the imagined return, restoring them should also improve plan choice beyond a matched random patch. To test this, we rank eight plans from each of 150 emulator states, as a sampling-based planner does [11, 20], and score pairwise accuracy and normalised top-1 regret; 7 of the twelve pairs, including the diffusion model, pass the reliability rules (supplement), and Fig. 7 shows one. The event patch improves pairwise accuracy in all 7 pairs, whereas a random patch changes it by a median of +0.019, and median top-1 regret falls from 0.565 to 0.141. Under pre-specified rules, 15 further games add 8 pairs from Freeway, CrazyClimber and Gopher, whose detectors also pass on plan states, and the event patch improves all 8 of them (median +0.156, random +0.012; supplement). On Pong, the diffusion model raises pairwise accuracy from 0.5000 to 0.6110 (random-weighted control 0.5007). The transitions carrying the return error thus also decide plan selection.

7 Cross-Task Transfer and Discussion

Beyond Atari, we apply the diagnostic to six DeepMind Control tasks and robosuite, and compare matched-action rollouts on MiniGrid and Crafter (Fig. 7). On the control tasks of Fig. 3, the three comparisons whose detector passes yield +54/+54 points of lift on sparse cartpole across two architectures and +8 on ball-in-cup (supplement).

Concurrent work finds ball disappearance and invalid ball–paddle interactions in five frozen Pong world models [34]; we locate the return error across 26 games.

8 Conclusion

In this paper, we introduce a per-transition substitution diagnostic that locates where the imagined return of a world model goes wrong. In 39 of 44 reliably measured model–collection pairs on Atari-100k, the return error concentrates at reward and termination transitions that pixel metrics do not single out: world models get the return wrong at events, in frames that look no worse than the rest. A rule recorded in advance predicts where a diffusion model class helps, and event patches improve plan ranking in every counted pair; the same concentration appears on control tasks with rare reward events. These results suggest evaluating world models for planning by where their return error occurs, in addition to how well they render frames.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
